name: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
aliases: juvenile gout with choreoathetosis and self-mutilation

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder caused by variants in HPRT1, encoding hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, so it almost exclusively affects males
Loss of purine salvage drives overproduction of uric acid, causing hyperuricaemia, hyperuricosuria, gout and urate nephrolithiasis
The complete deficiency (classic Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) produces a triad of hyperuricaemia, a dystonic-choreoathetoid movement disorder and compulsive self-injurious behaviour
Self-mutilation, typically biting of the lips and fingers, is a distinctive and highly characteristic feature
Early clues include orange 'sand' (urate crystals) in the nappy and delayed motor development with evolving dystonia
Partial HPRT deficiency (Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome) causes hyperuricaemia and gout with little or no neurological involvement
Urate-lowering therapy controls the systemic complications but does not improve the neurological or behavioural features
Protective measures and behavioural strategies are needed to prevent self-inflicted injury
reference.pathophysiology: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase catalyses the salvage of the purine bases hypoxanthine and guanine back into nucleotides. When the enzyme is deficient, salvage fails and the purine bases are instead degraded to uric acid, while de novo purine synthesis is disinhibited; the combined effect is marked uric acid overproduction with hyperuricaemia and its complications. The neurological and behavioural phenotype is less well understood but is linked to dysfunction of dopaminergic pathways in the basal ganglia, which correlates with the dystonia, choreoathetosis and compulsive self-injury. The severity of the phenotype tracks closely with the amount of residual enzyme activity.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of childhood dystonia and choreoathetosis
Primary or secondary hyperuricaemia and juvenile gout
Autism spectrum disorder with self-injurious behaviour
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urine uric acid with the urinary urate-to-creatinine ratio
HPRT enzyme activity assay in erythrocytes or fibroblasts
Renal tract imaging for urate stones and nephrocalcinosis
redFlags: Evolving dystonia with developmental delay in a young boy
Urate crystals or stones with renal impairment
Acute urate nephropathy or obstructive uropathy
reference.prognosis: Systemic urate complications can be controlled with urate-lowering therapy, preventing gout and nephropathy, but the neurological and behavioural features of the complete syndrome are not reversible and cause lifelong disability. Life expectancy is reduced, with renal failure and complications of the movement and behavioural disorder contributing to mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming that urate-lowering therapy will improve neurological or behavioural symptoms
Misdiagnosing the movement disorder as dyskinetic cerebral palsy
Overlooking hyperuricaemia as a diagnostic clue in a boy with dystonia and self-injury
Failing to implement protective measures against self-mutilation
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Urate-lowering therapy with the xanthine oxidase inhibitor allopurinol to prevent gout, urate nephrolithiasis and urate nephropathy
Generous fluid intake and urinary alkalinisation to reduce urate and xanthine stone formation
Treatment of the dystonic-choreoathetoid movement disorder with agents such as baclofen and benzodiazepines
Prevention of self-injurious behaviour with protective devices, lip and dental guards, sometimes dental extraction, alongside behavioural therapy
Multidisciplinary care involving neurology, metabolic medicine, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychiatry
Monitoring of renal function and imaging surveillance for urate stones and nephrocalcinosis
Genetic counselling and carrier testing for this X-linked recessive HPRT1 disorder
